title: Three bad months
eyebrow: CETI case · streaks in random sequences
lede: Sales fell three months in a row. Before anyone looks for a cause, look at what a fair coin does: in 100 flips, a run of seven of the same side turns up more often than not.

commit.title: LONGEST RUN
commit.prompt: In 100 fair coin flips, what is the longest run of the same side in a row?

captions: Sales fell three months in a row.
The room says: something is wrong. Is it?
First, a coin. Flip it 100 times. Pure chance.
Longest run of one side in a row? Pick a number.
1985: Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky ask 100 fans.
91 of 100: likelier to score after 2 or 3 hits than misses.
Hits 50 of 100? Fans guess 61 after a hit, 42 after a miss.
76ers, 1980–81: no sign that hits bred more hits.
Now pure coin flips: 100 per row, up or down.
Ten rows. The longest run in each one is boxed.
1,000 rows of pure chance, stacked by longest run.
7 or more: 546 of 1,000. Your number sits on the same pile.
Monday: would a coin flip have made this streak too?
Limit: chance makes streaks. A hot hand may still exist.

brand.takeaway: Chance makes streaks. Ask what a coin would have done.

sources: Gilovich, T., Vallone, R., & Tversky, A. (1985). The hot hand in basketball: On the misperception of random sequences. Cognitive Psychology, 17(3), 295–314. doi:10.1016/0010-0285(85)90010-6
Miller, J. B., & Sanjurjo, A. (2018). Surprised by the hot hand fallacy? A truth in the law of small numbers. Econometrica, 86(6), 2019–2047. doi:10.3982/ECTA14943
Schilling, M. F. (1990). The longest run of heads. The College Mathematics Journal, 21(3), 196–207. doi:10.2307/2686886
Tversky, A., & Kahneman, D. (1971). Belief in the law of small numbers. Psychological Bulletin, 76(2), 105–110. doi:10.1037/h0031322

This film's computation: exact recursion over every 100-flip sequence; seeded simulation mulberry32 (seed 1985 for the 1,000 rows, 140 for the 12-month strip, 1 for a 100,000-trial check). Formulas in claims.json.
honest: Chance makes streaks; that does not prove the hot hand is a myth. Miller and Sanjurjo (2018) found a bias in the 1985 test: in a finite record, the share of hits right after a streak of hits is expected to fall below the base rate even when shots are independent (in 100 fair flips, 0.46 after three heads, not 0.50). Corrected, the data allow a modest hot hand.
Real sales months are not coin flips: trend, seasonality and momentum are real. The coin is the comparison to make before acting, not a diagnosis that your business is random.

The 12-month strip in the hook was picked from seeded coin flips to end on three falls. The 1,000 rows are one seeded stream (mulberry32, seed 1985), not hand-picked; their counts differ slightly from the exact odds (546 vs 542 expected for 7 or more).
